articles.title: Businessman at centre of Thurrock Council scandal tracked to Bucharest
articles.summary: Reporters find Liam Kavanagh at an exclusive apartment complex in Bucharest.
articles.body:
The BBC has tracked down businessman Liam Kavanagh to a luxury apartment in Bucharest. His whereabouts had remained largely unknown for years following his role in one of the biggest financial scandals in British local government history.

Thurrock Council in Essex invested more than £600m in Kavanagh's solar energy businesses - despite stark warnings that the investments were too risky.

With the money he received, Kavanagh bought a £12m private jet, a yacht, a fleet of supercars, a country house adored by Jane Austen, a Damien Hirst pickled sheep artwork and a £250,000 revolving bed.

Then it all came crashing down. Thurrock was left with a vast financial black hole and effectively went bankrupt, forcing central government to step in with hundreds of millions of pounds of taxpayers' money.

The council is now suing Kavanagh, accusing him of deceit and alleging that millions of pounds of its investments were diverted for his personal benefit.

Kavanagh denies misleading Thurrock and any wrongdoing. His legal defence says he honestly believed he was entitled to use the money in the way he did and highlights wording which he claims allowed him to make deductions from the money Thurrock invested.

At the heart of the story are two seemingly very different men.

Kavanagh, known by some as Mr Sunshine, was the charismatic businessman selling investments in solar farms. Sean Clark was Thurrock's finance director - the council official who found the money to invest with him.

He borrowed huge sums from other local authorities around the UK, often through deals that could be arranged with a few emails. At one point Thurrock owed more than £1bn to other councils.

The strategy initially appeared to be a triumph. The investments were generating millions of pounds in income at a time when councils were struggling with government spending cuts.

But behind the apparent success, warning signs were mounting.

Journalist Gareth Davies, of the Bureau of Investigative Journalism, has spent years investigating what happened.

"I think this story is so shocking because of the scale of the greed, of the incompetence - the fact that this council gambled with huge sums of public money and lost."

Describing the lack of records surrounding some of the deals, Davies said: "There wasn't even evidence at the time that these transactions were made, that any of this had ever taken place. I mean, it's mind-boggling."

Thurrock's own financial adviser, Arlingclose, was also sounding the alarm.

Arlingclose chief executive Mark Pickering described the council's investment activity as "pretty extreme" and said his firm felt "the likelihood of them blowing up was pretty high".

"You try several times to help a friend - and after a while you have to leave them to their own devices, don't you?" he said.

Arlingclose eventually cut ties with Thurrock. But Clark carried on borrowing and investing.

Meanwhile, leaked bank records show millions moving from Kavanagh's company into his personal accounts, alongside payments for luxury purchases.

He also started to look like a different man after Thurrock's investments.

"You can look in terms of the photographs, before and after," said Davies.

"At one end you've got a fairly unkempt man whose nickname in the early days was the sticky Bandit because he looked like one of the bad guys out of Home Alone.

"A few years later - this bronzed, muscular man who's obviously enjoying a luxury lifestyle."

For six years, Kavanagh avoided answering many of the key questions about what happened.

So we went looking for him, and eventually traced him to an exclusive apartment complex in northern Bucharest.

Leaked financial records give a glimpse of the life inside: One wall covered in Swarovski crystals, another featuring 25 television screens, and the enormous revolving bed - so big it had to be lifted into the penthouse by crane.

We attempted to deliver Kavanagh a letter containing our questions and asked him to come downstairs to sign for it. We wanted him to come in person so we could ask him our questions.

He did not appear. Soon afterwards, a security guard carrying a camera was stationed outside the building.

Kavanagh's lawyers later confirmed we had found the correct address and said he did not wish to communicate with us directly.

BBC reporters approached him near his home in Kent while he was walking his dog and asked whether it was OK if we asked some questions about Thurrock.

Asked whether he felt any guilt, or had anything to say to the people of Thurrock, Clark answered simply: "No."

He also declined to answer why he had invested so much public money with one businessman, or whether he was "a fool or a crook".

Clark has admitted professional misconduct relating to his time at Thurrock. The Financial Reporting Council said he had "recklessly provided misleading information to council members, and therefore to the public". He received a severe reprimand and was excluded from membership of his professional accountancy body for five years.

The Serious Fraud Office is investigating suspected fraud involving Kavanagh's businesses and Thurrock Council. It has not announced whether Kavanagh will face criminal charges.

For the people of Thurrock, however, the bill has already arrived - through higher council tax, reduced services and debts that will burden the authority for years.

Local charity worker Neil Woodbridge became emotional when we asked him about the lack of accountability.

"I can't get my head around the fact that no-one's held to account," he said.

articles.title: Bulldog suffering severe infection saved by Coventry animal rescue
articles.summary: But rescue owner says that dog abandonments are on the rise and "out of hand"
articles.body:
A foster dog rescue helped save a bulldog suffering from a severe bacterial infection which had spread across his body.

Gemma Kirby, founder of New Leash of Life in Coventry, said George came into the organisation's care around six weeks ago after his owner was no longer able to care for him or get him to veterinary appointments.

The seven-year-old dog is now on the road to recovery and looking for a new home.

The rescue recently helped another dog Trevor, a five-year-old Labrador, after his owners asked a veterinary practice in Nuneaton to put him to sleep because he was too energetic around children. It currently has about 15 dogs in foster homes and said dog abandonment cases were rising.

Kirby said up her foundation in April and is currently waiting to get premises.

"George is one of the worst cases I have seen medically come through the door. But seeing his transformation shows why we do what we do. We have sleepless nights, we cry, and these dogs mean the world to us."

She said: "The number of abandonment cases is terrible now. It has got so much worse.

"People aren't doing their research and are getting breeds whose needs they can't meet. It has got out of hand."

She said it is "angering and exhausting" but then there are positive stories such as George.

"If we hadn't have got involved, that dog could have died or been left in a terrible situation," she said.

George remains on medication and is continuing to make good progress.

An appeal has been launched to help cover his treatment costs and any future surgery.

Kirby said: "Even though they are not our dogs initially, they become part of our family. It is so important to us to do everything we can to make sure they are comfortable, happy and loved."

The rescue recently helped Trevor, a five-year-old Labrador, after his owners asked a veterinary practice in Nuneaton to put him to sleep because he was too energetic around children.

"The vet said no, we're not doing that. He was a healthy and really lovely boy," Kirby said.

After finding him a foster placement, Trevor moved into his permanent home on Sunday.

"If we hadn't found him a foster space, there would have been nowhere for Trevor to go."

articles.title: Wellingborough 'hogspital' founder saddened by intake pause
articles.summary: Val Saunders says she is looking after 24 very ill hoglets when she would normally limit it to 16.
articles.body:
The founder of a "hogspital" says she feels "exhausted and sad" that she has had to close hedgehog admissions.

Val Saunders, who runs Hoggieworts Hedgehog Helpers, in Wellingborough, Northamptonshire, said she has been "completely overwhelmed by the avalanche of tiny hedgehogs arriving".

She said she ideally had space for 16 hedgehogs, but as she was currently caring for 24 it meant she could not take in any more.

Animals In Need, a Northamptonshire-based charity, said it was also "inundated" and was currently caring for about 50 animals.

Saunders, 66, said she built her self-funded "hogspital" about two years ago because she loves the animals "to bits".

It has 16 pods but she said "it's hard work at my age".

"I've noticed the difference in the past 10 years, 16 is enough I can deal with.

"We've had an avalanche of them in the past four weeks, some really sick, poorly babies.

"We're splitting at the seams. It's exhausting, so sad, I'm just left frustrated."

She believed the influx of hoglets was down to a long hot summer and then a recent sharp drop in the temperature.

"I think mums have pushed out their litters later when the babies were not weaned before they were going into hibernation.

"The lack of food has been a perfect storm for all the little ones."

She also said she was dealing with a high number of the mammals with parasites, such as fluke, coccidia and lung and round worm.

Saunders said she makes sure she cares for the really sick hedgehogs but any that just need help putting on weight before they are released are sent to her team of foster carers.

"I would take in more but it's not about the space, it's the time, I have to be able to provide a good service."

A spokesperson for Animals in Need said it was not turning any hedgehogs away.

They said it had put its influx also down to the hot summer that "messed mother nature up".

They confirmed that at its peak they had looked after up to 200 hedgehogs but currently they were looking after lots of hoglets that were "underweight".

articles.title: I sang carols to the Ghost of Christmas Present – and Johnny Depp
articles.summary: Colin Fraser, from Barton-le-Clay, says it was "amazing" to be a singer in the new Ebenezer film.
articles.body:
A musician who usually performs on movie soundtracks says it is "surreal" to be on-screen singing carols in Ebenezer – the latest film adaptation of A Christmas Carol.

"There's a pivotal scene in a prison yard, and we're singing Silent Night with the Ghost of Christmas Present and Johnny Depp there," recalls Bedfordshire's Colin Fraser.

Depp plays the title character Ebenezer Scrooge in the Charles Dickens tale, starring alongside Rupert Grint, Sir Ian McKellen and Daisy Ridley.

Fraser, 55, who has appeared in West End shows such as The Lion King, landed his current role when London Voices, his choir, was asked to audition for the film.

He says that despite the spooky setting, the renditions of Silent Night and other carols are "completely straight" and "very traditional".

"We sang them traditionally in four-part harmony as we would every year," he says.

"There's a street scene and we're around the Christmas tree, singing – I think it was I Saw Three Ships Come Sailing In.

"There was all the snow being pumped in and it felt like a very traditional Christmas."

As part of London Voices, Fraser is often "at Abbey Road or Air Studios recording film soundtracks, such as the Marvel films, Wonka, James Bond".

But the opportunity to perform in front of the camera on a major Hollywood production was "bizarre – we were really shocked".

"Normally, we would be singing on the soundtrack, but... for our faces to be in it – it's quite amazing," he says.

He adds that the carol singing in Ebenezer was "all done live, not pre-recorded in the studio" – and the same went for the setting.

"The sets were incredible. There's no kind of CGI or anything like that. We weren't singing on green screens," says Fraser, from Barton-le-Clay, on the Hertfordshire border.

"They transformed this area. It looked rough and dirty, the peasants were peeling potatoes and warming themselves by fires."

Making a Christmas film set meant several winter night shoots

"It was probably around one o'clock in the morning in February, and it started raining," Fraser says.

"We've got the full gamut of cold British weather. It was quite poignant being on that set."

The singers would perform for "five, maybe six hours" through the night.

"It gives you a real idea of how hard it is to be a film actor, because you have to give a massive performance every single time," he says.

Ti West, known for horror films, is a "very hands-on" director, says Fraser.

"He was operating cameras. He's very involved in it all.

"He wasn't sitting back on a chair somewhere shouting at people. He's very much [in] everything."

Fraser says he hopes "another film will come up, because it's very interesting to be on the set".

He adds: "It was surreal. It was really good. There was the rain while you're singing Silent Night – it was full of a lot of emotions."

articles.title: In 1981, Virginia recycled 7.85 miles of Route 220 into new asphalt using about 40% of the old road; two years later, the Franklin County pavement was performing well
articles.summary: Discover how Virginia paved the way for sustainable road construction in 1981 by recycling 40% of asphalt on Route 220, achieving impressive durability and performance.
articles.body: Road construction often involves removing damaged pavement and replacing it with new material. Engineers can also use recycled asphalt in order to create a new road surface as well. Virginia used this approach in three earlier projects in central Virginia, according to the Virginia Highway and Transportation Research Council, before it recycled a 7.85-mile stretch of US Route 220 in Franklin County in the fall of 1981. This project involved a 7.85-mile section of the road and included about 40% recycled pavement in the asphalt mixture. Engineers needed to evaluate whether used road material could be treated in a regular asphalt mixing plant and still serve under usual traffic conditions. The assessment conducted in 1984 confirmed that the used asphalt served quite well for about two years.Virginia reused 40% of the old pavement on Route 220The construction of Route 220 represented an extension of Virginia’s earlier efforts in asphalt recycling. The state had undertaken other hot mix recycling programmes prior to undertaking this major demonstration program. According to Hughes’s 1982 installation report, milling started on September 8, 1981, in the northbound lanes of US Route 220 in Franklin County. This was done because the base course of asphalt was in very good condition. Charles S. Hughes documented the construction process in the Virginia Highway and Transportation Research Council’s Installation Report: Evaluation of Recycled Hot Mix Asphaltic Concrete on Route 220, published in 1982. The report describes a project covering roughly 8 miles of roadway, where the top two asphalt layers were milled, recycled through a conventional batch plant and relaid. The finished mix used about 40% reclaimed material and 60% virgin aggregate and the work went ahead with little difficulty.The recovered asphalt was processed and incorporated into a new hot mixture. The final mix was 40% reclaimed pavement material and 60% virgin aggregate, which was a blend of granite and sand. About 3.0% AC-5 asphalt cement was added on top of that, as detailed in the research report. Hughes’s installation report says paving began on September 30 and was completed on October 28, 1981. The installation report says the project included the full width of both northbound lanes, from north of Rocky Mount to south of Boones Mill.Engineers modified an existing asphalt plant to process reclaimed materialThe process involved the modification of an ordinary asphalt batch plant. Engineers included the installation of a bin and elevator to allow the transfer of the reclaimed pavement through the entire process. In addition, the materials went through a two-inch screen to eliminate the larger particles before going into the plant. In laboratory tests, the result indicated that the asphalt binder was highly rigid, especially the ones in the top layers of the pavement. This problem was sorted out by using softer AC-5 asphalt binder in the new mix. Finally, the project also resulted in the creation of excess materials beyond the needs of Route 220. Some of the excess materials were used for overlaying Route 40 in Franklin County. The initial use of cold recycled mix with CMS-2 emulsion was unsuccessful and therefore, the rest was done using hot recycled mix.A two-year evaluation found satisfactory pavement performanceHughes examined the road’s condition in the 1984 report. Two-Year Evaluation of Recycled Hot Mix Asphalt Concrete on Route 220: Interim Report. The evaluation consisted of a comparison of the data collected during the construction of the road with those obtained one and two years after service. The characteristics of the asphalt did not vary much within the period. The air voids in the mixture decreased due to compaction or the sealing of the pavement by traffic. The surface texture increased slightly while the present serviceability index fell a bit. Skid resistance went up over the period of two years.The report stated that the recycled pavement had been doing well, two years after it had been laid. A later three-year assessment, Evaluation of Recycled Hot Mix Asphalt Concrete on Route 220: Final Report, published in 1985, reported very good pavement performance. These results also led Virginia to consider a specification for using up to 25% recycled materials in the manufacturing process of hot mix asphalt by contractors. Thus, the Franklin County case study was an example of successful use of reclaimed asphalt in the construction of highway pavements for several years.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Venâncio Mondlane: Mozambique opposition leader goes on trial amid tension in Maputo
articles.summary: Venâncio Mondlane faces several charges over 2024 post-election protests that left hundreds of people dead.
articles.body:
Tensions are running high in Mozambique's capital, Maputo, with a heavy police deployment as a prominent opposition leader goes on trial over deadly protests that followed the country's disputed 2024 elections.

Venâncio Mondlane faces several charges, including incitement to terrorism and civil disobedience, over protests that left hundreds of people dead. He denies any wrongdoing.

Security has been tightened around the Supreme Court, where Mondlane is due to appear on Tuesday, with authorities fearing a fresh wave of demonstrations by his supporters.

Police have appealed to citizens to follow the proceedings calmly and avoid actions that could threaten public order.

Mondlane arrived at the Supreme Court early on Tuesday with "great peace of mind", and was greeted by dozens of supporters.

"As you can see, I arrive calm, confident in the work of my legal team," he told journalists gathered outside court, amid a heavy police presence.

The trial is widely seen as a major test of Mozambique's political stability, nearly two years after disputed elections triggered some of the country's deadliest political unrest in decades.

"The trial is a real test for Mozambique. It is is an important opportunity to demonstrate that the rule of law applies equally to everyone," said Luis Nhachote, a political analyst.

Mondlane, who challenged the presidential election results that declared Daniel Chapo of the ruling Frelimo party the winner, accused the authorities of widespread electoral fraud and called for nationwide protests and work stoppages.

Children shot dead after joining pot-banging protests in Mozambique

The demonstrations continued for months, with rights groups accusing security forces of using excessive force against protesters.

Amnesty International, citing local civil society organisations, said more than 300 people were killed during the unrest, which was one of the country's worst post-election crises since independence.

Mozambican police put the death toll at 96, including 17 police officers.

European Union election observers also reported irregularities in the October 2024 vote, raising questions about the credibility of the results.

Prosecutors accuse Mondlane of encouraging demonstrations that disrupted public services, damaged property and threatened public security.

The charges include publicly glorifying criminal acts, incitement to collective disobedience, public instigation to commit crimes and offences linked to terrorism.

He could face up to 24 years in prison if convicted of the most serious charge.

Mondlane has rejected the accusations, insisting that his calls for demonstrations were aimed at demanding electoral transparency rather than encouraging violence.

His party, the National Alliance for a Free and Autonomous Mozambique (Anamola), has described the prosecution as politically motivated.

The Supreme Court has denied allegations of political interference in the proceedings.

A heavy deployment of police has been seen patrolling around the Supreme Court and major streets in Maputo ahead of the trial.

In a statement issued on Monday, Mozambique's police appealed to citizens to "preserve tolerance and peaceful coexistence," adding that the right to demonstrate must be exercised strictly within the limits of the law.

Police also pledged to protect people and property while acting preventively and proportionately in accordance with the rule of law.

The court has only granted access to selected media organisations, sparking criticism from journalists and press freedom campaigners.

Court officials say the restrictions are necessary because of limited seating capacity in the courtroom, but critics argue they undermine transparency in a case of significant public interest.

The proceedings are expected to be heard by five judges, with witnesses called by both the prosecution and defence.

Political observers warn that the trial could reignite tensions in a country still struggling to recover from the violence and deep political divisions that followed the 2024 elections.

articles.title: Outdoor instructor prepares for 'coolest' Christmas in Antarctica
articles.summary: Shrewsbury adventurer Oli Wilde's wild life takes another turn as he prepares to spend Christmas in Antarctica.
articles.body:
An outdoor instructor is preparing to swap the familiar landscapes of Shropshire for the icebergs and wildlife of Antarctica.

Oli Wilde, from Shrewsbury, will leave the UK next week to begin work as an expedition guide, leading visitors on kayaking trips and wildlife excursions across the Antarctic Peninsula and beyond the Antarctic Circle.

The 14-day expeditions will also see him working over Christmas aboard a luxury expedition ship, taking passengers out in smaller boats to explore glaciers, spot whales and encounter penguins and seals.

"I've never really seen big mammals like the blue whale and humpback whale," he said, adding: "They're just huge. So I think seeing one of those is going to be pretty incredible."

Wilde is due back on 12 January, meaning he will spend Christmas on the ship.

"I think it's just going to be probably one of the coolest Christmases I've ever done," he said.

The opportunity marks a new chapter for Wilde, who has spent the past few years working as an outdoor instructor, having started in Pembrokeshire.

His work has involved coasteering and sea kayaking during the day, often followed by rock climbing in the evenings.

He said: "I'm just going out and having fun getting paid. And what's really cool is to develop; you just go out and have fun, and that's how you improve."

Wilde has been preparing for the new role by learning about the animals he could encounter, including the region's large populations of seabirds, seals and penguins.

He said he had a particular passion for wildlife and had enjoyed learning about the environment while working in Wales.

"I've got a huge passion for animals," he said.

"When I was working in Pembrokeshire, I really enjoyed learning about the environment and the animals that live in it.

"The animals they have in Antarctica, they're just incredible. So I'm finding it quite interesting just learning, learning everything about them."

As an expedition guide, he will be responsible for keeping passengers safe and ensuring they respect the wildlife and its habitat.

"One of the main things is managing the boats around icebergs because it's super easy for them to roll," he explained.

"It would be really bad if you're right beside them."

Guides also need to be aware of leopard seals, which Wilde described as "apex predators", and ensure kayakers keep a safe distance from wildlife.

The expeditions will begin in Ushuaia, at the southern tip of Argentina, before sailing across open water to Antarctica.

Wilde will work aboard the MS Roald Amundsen, a hybrid expedition ship with more than 400 passenger spaces. He will use Zodiac speedboats and sea kayaks to take groups out exploring.

Although excited, Wilde admitted he felt some pressure about taking on a new job with a highly sought-after expedition company.

"I think it's natural to be nervous about going to a new job, but I think especially for a company that's highly sought after.

"You're doing a trip which is quite expensive per person, so I feel the pressure because I want to be the best instructor I can be and have all the knowledge ready.

"So in that way, I definitely feel a little bit nervous, and I do feel the pressure, but the only way to get over that is just to get really good at learning all the information about the animals and be myself.

And while he is hoping to encounter some of the world's largest animals, there is another childhood ambition he is particularly keen to fulfil.

Talking about the penguins he hopes to see, he said: "It's going to live up to my childhood dream after watching Happy Feet."

articles.title: Harvard study estimates magnitude of U.S. data center pollution as climate talks unveil clean AI pledge
articles.summary: The 400 largest data centers in the United States put more heat-trapping gas in the air in one year than the entire nation of Denmark did, and that was before the artificial intelligence boom really got going, according to a Harvard University study.
articles.body: The 400 largest data centers in the United States put more heat-trapping gas in the air in one year than the entire nation of Denmark did, and that was before the artificial intelligence boom really got going, according to a Harvard University study published Monday. Meanwhile, negotiators at the United Nations COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, launched a voluntary pledge Monday for companies and countries to power the world’s data centers with clean energy and be more open about their power and water consumption and emissions. “We cannot ask people to accept higher bills, more planet heating pollution and deeper inequality today in exchange for promises of a better tomorrow,” United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell said Monday during the launch of the pledge. “Claims about future emissions savings cannot excuse rising pollution now, making climate disasters even worse.” The pledge also calls for focusing the power of artificial intelligence on solving the so-far intractable problem of climate change and reflects burgeoning concerns about AI’s ever-expanding environmental footprint. The political backlash has played out in U.S. elections and major local objections for new sites. The explosion of new and planned data centers also has prompted a push for new sources of power generation that has the biggest tech companies failing to reach their climate goals, with their electricity consumption rising 240% between 2022 and 2025, according to a new report by the advocacy group Climate Action Against Disinformation. Study quantifies how much big data centers pollute Harvard researchers looked at 403 of the largest U.S. data centers between May 2024 and April 2025 using available data and modeling to analyze their electricity use and emissions. They estimated electricity use by the centers produced around 28.3 million tons (25.7 million metric tons) of carbon dioxide, according to a study in Monday’s Nature Sustainability. More than half their 82 terawatt hours of electricity use — enough to power nearly 7 million homes for a year — came from fossil fuels, which are the primary cause of global warming, the researchers found. The emissions estimate is two to three times what previous studies had shown, said study senior author Francesca Dominici, a Harvard biostatistics professor. “It is the equivalent to the CO2 emission of an entire state like Michigan or a small European country,” Dominici said, adding that plans for 2,000 more data centers make that quantity more worrisome for the future. “We are going backwards toward the goal of controlling CO2 emissions.” Several outside experts in climate, energy and artificial intelligence said Monday’s study made sense and reached realistic conclusions, finding the use of modeling reasonable because companies aren’t open about power consumption and pollution. “We cannot manage environmental impacts effectively without reliable measurements and disclosure,” said Fengqi You, a Cornell University energy systems scientist who wasn’t part of the study. “Ultimately, the environmental footprint of AI is not fixed. It depends on where we build data centers, how efficiently they operate, and how we supply their electricity.” A voluntary pledge proposed at climate talks The “Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge,” launched by U.N. climate talks host Turkey and the International Telecommunication Union, says data centers should use clean power and efficient energy and water systems. The pledge also calls for AI systems to be designed and managed responsibly, using environmental standards and reusing or recycling infrastructure and hardware. It says the environmental impacts of data centers should be assessed and shared and signatories should support using artificial intelligence as a climate solution. COP31 President Murat Kurum has said world leaders at the talks must openly discuss AI’s growing energy consumption and start setting the terms. AI produces pollution but also offers hope One of the biggest climate fighters, former U.S. Vice President Al Gore, said while it is essential that data centers are powered by carbon-free energy, he is less concerned about the emissions from AI than others. And he is hopeful that its computing power can find novel ways of fighting climate change. In an Associated Press interview, Gore quoted a study by prominent British economist and climate advocate Nicholas Stern who predicted by 2030 “we will see 6 to 9% reduction in emissions of greenhouse gases because of the use of advanced AI in finding new ways to be far more efficient in the use of materials and energy.” Caleb Max, president of the National Artificial Intelligence Association said, “AI will solve not only the energy usage issues that data centers face, but unlock numerous currently unknown advances in science and technology that will address climate change and make lives better for humanity. I respect the concerns about energy and water consumption from data centers, but the fears may be overblown.” But Climate Action Against Disinformation spokesman Philip Newell was skeptical. “We have hope in one hand and then harms in the other,” Newell said. “They’re selling us hope while hiding the harms from us.” Capturing heat from data centers The computing equipment in data centers generates a lot of waste heat that is vented into the atmosphere. One approach to reducing data centers’ environmental impact is to capture heat that can be used for nearby homes and businesses. The Danish engineering and manufacturing company Danfoss said waste heat is “the world’s largest untapped energy source,” and reusing it can replace natural gas as a heat source. It identified data centers as a significant source of constant heat, particularly as their power consumption grows. The International Energy Agency estimates data centers could provide enough heat for around 10% of European homes by 2030, if that heat was fully integrated into district systems that supply heat and hot water to residents. In remarks broadcast during COP31, European Commissioner for Energy and Housing Dan Jørgensen said Europe must replace imported fossil fuels by capturing heat that is going to waste and tapping into geothermal. In another example of this approach, industrial development firm BaRupOn is building an advanced manufacturing campus in Texas that plans to use recaptured heat to generate additional electricity on site, CEO Balaji Tammabattula said. In North Dakota, the company is planning a data center that could feed heat to the community. University of Colorado Boulder Professor Gregor Henze said it’s a perfect marriage because modern data centers that rely on liquid rather than air cooling are a fairly constant source of heat at the right temperature for thermal energy networks.

articles.title: 'Order passed without hearing me': Bilkis Bano to challenge SC order granting bail to two convicts
articles.summary: VADODARA: Bilkis Bano has said she will challenge the Supreme Court's October 28 order suspending the sentences and granting bail to two of the 11 men
articles.body: VADODARA: Bilkis Bano has said she will challenge the Supreme Court's October 28 order suspending the sentences and granting bail to two of the 11 men convicted of gang-raping her and murdering 14 members of her family during the 2002 Gujarat riots.In a statement issued through senior advocate Shobha Gupta, she expressed shock and disbelief that the order was passed without informing her or giving her an opportunity to be heard.Bilkis said she learnt about the development through press reports and questioned how the Supreme Court could pass such an order without ensuring that her voice was heard. She said this was the second time an order concerning the case had been passed without calling her or hearing her."I still cannot believe that once again, for the second time, an order has been passed by the Supreme Court without calling me up and without hearing me. I learnt of this through press reports," she said.Recalling the horrific events of 2002, Bilkis said she was just 19 years old when her world, her baby daughter, family, home and trust in humanity were brutally wrenched away from her. For the past 24 years, she said, she had fought repeatedly for justice, not only for herself but also for women everywhere.She said she had discovered reserves of courage she never knew she possessed, largely because of the support and solidarity extended by a million voices. She recalled walking from one courtroom to another and being grateful each time she was vindicated and her faith in the idea of justice was restored.Bilkis said she had gradually rebuilt her life with the love and support of family and friends, yearned for peace and learnt to smile. However, the latest order had left her feeling that she was losing the very justice she had fought so hard to secure.She said familiar fears had resurfaced and she was scared once again for herself, her family and her children. She also expressed apprehension about losing faith in the justice system yet again.Questioning the decision to suspend the sentences of the men convicted in the case, she asked how the court could have passed the order without informing her or ensuring that she was heard."I will fight this order. I must," she said, adding that her fight was for her children, who did not deserve to remain haunted by the fears and scars of the past for the rest of their lives.She also invoked the memory of her three-year-old daughter Saleha, who was killed during the 2002 violence, saying she deserved to live and that her memory demanded justice.Bilkis said her fight was also for women everywhere, asserting that no woman, survivor or citizen should have to endure an eternal test of belonging and equality or spend the rest of her life fighting for justice.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Woman who accuses Russell Brand of rape says prison message 'upsetting'
articles.summary: Mia Latter spoke to the BBC after the jailed comedian claimed he was innocent of offences against four other women, in comments on a podcast following his convction.
articles.body:
A woman who has made allegations against Russell Brand has said she finds it "upsetting" and "really shocking" that he was able to claim he was innocent from prison , following his conviction for rape and sexual assault.

Speaking after the comedian's wife Laura read out a message from him on their Sunday Service show on YouTube, Mia Latter told BBC Radio 4's Today programme she found it "appalling" to hear "this Christian message alongside absolute lies".

"I just felt for those women that stood trial and everything they went through," she said.

Latter, 37, who has alleged she was raped by Brand when she was 16, was not a complainant in his recent criminal trial and he denies her claims.

Brand is currently serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after being found guilty at Southwark Crown Court of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, involving four women.

In recent years he has positioned himself as a Christian influencer, and has a large following, including in the US. In the message read out by his wife on their show, Brand said: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."

Latter said the broadcast "was really shocking to me... it was appalling, frankly, it was upsetting to watch".

She said the woman who gave evidence in the trial "got their verdict, and for him to say, 'I'm innocent, I'm not guilty' - well, you are, you're a convicted rapist now. There's no arguing with that".

Downing Street said on Monday it expects action to be taken if Brand is found to have broken prison rules.

Justice Secretary Alex Norris said that "prisoners are rightly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims".

Latter said she was 16 when she met Brand, who was 30 at the time.

She was one of six women who made allegations against him as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation in 2023. None of the women were involved in his recent trial.

In an interview with the Sunday Times this week, Latter said Brand told her to keep their relationship secret from her school friends and claimed that he referred to her as "the child" in front of his entourage.

She has waived her right to anonymity in order to campaign for a staggered age of consent to be introduced in the UK that would make sexual relationships between 16 and 17 year-olds and adults illegal.

Latter told the Sunday Times the Crown Prosecution Service decided not to include her as part of Brand's criminal trial but police wanted her to be part of "subsequent" proceedings. She told the paper that she would not continue with the criminal process so she could focus on her campaign.

Russell Brand prison message 'appalling' and being investigated, No 10 says

Brand moved from Wandsworth to category C prison, his wife confirms on podcast

Alleged Russell Brand rape victim wants age of consent law changed

Latter told Today a staggered age of consent could have stopped her relationship with Brand "dead in its tracks".

She said: "It would have 100% made a difference because my parents tried to stop the relationship.

"They tried to prevent me from seeing him... But if it had been a criminal offence for him to be having a relationship with me, none of the subsequent abuse would have ever happened because they would have been able to stop the relationship dead in its tracks."

Latter also told Today that she and the complainants in Brand's trial had been accused of being "money hungry".

She said she had initially been reluctant to speak out because "I knew that the audience that he'd cultivated over the past few years would come for me".

"It's a criminal trial, there's no money.

"Me talking to the Times, me talking to you, me doing any interviews, there's no money, there's not a penny. We're just doing this in the pursuit of justice."

But Latter said Brand had been "monetising all these platforms" during his trial by continuing to make videos that appeared with advertisements on social media.

articles.title: A woman remortgaged her home and sent £130,000 to a Facebook stranger claiming to be a celebrity technology businessman; her family grew concerned after she stopped having enough money to buy food
articles.summary: A vulnerable woman lost a total of £130,000 to a Facebook fraudster who claimed to be a well-known celebrity technology businessman and promised to settle
articles.body: A vulnerable woman lost a total of £130,000 to a Facebook fraudster who claimed to be a well-known celebrity technology businessman and promised to settle down with her. Over two months, he claimed he planned to come to the United Kingdom but kept making numerous excuses, while she remortgaged her house and sent him money. The woman had said on her profile that she was interested in technology when the man first made contact. Her weekly pension stopped lasting because she was sending money to the scammer, and that was one of the signs that finally exposed the deception.Why a fake celebrity businessman via Facebook asked the woman to send moneyAccording to Staffordshire Police, the man claimed that his notoriety meant he could not use his own bank accounts to carry out his plans. He therefore asked the woman to send money from her account, saying he would return it.A family member noticed that her behaviour had changed, and her relatives also saw that she was not eating properly because she no longer had accessible cash to buy groceries. Even after the scam was revealed, the woman struggled to accept what had happened to her, and social services became involved to help with her finances.Truth or Trap: The campaign behind the warning and what the police fraud specialist told the publicThe force issued the warning in October 2025 as part of its Truth or Trap campaign, which highlights the signs of three major types of fraud, romance scams among them. Officers said at the time that they were continuing to investigate alongside colleagues at Action Fraud. Simon Street, the force’s fraud protect and prepare co-ordinator with its major and organised crime unit, told the public that although the case appears unusual, scams of this kind are sadly all too common. He added that fraudsters exploit any information that might make a person vulnerable, and that officers worked with partners to help the woman find the right support going forward.How romance scammers work and where to report concerns about yourself or someone you knowRomance scammers typically build elaborate stories to earn trust over time, then invent a problem in which the victim is the only person who can help, isolate them from family and friends and press for increasing amounts of money. Anyone worried about romance fraud, or who thinks someone they know may be a victim, can call the police on 101, use Livechat on its website or contact Action Fraud.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Michigan coal plant scheduled to shut down remains open under a seventh federal emergency order despite an appeals court ruling; environmental groups estimate the extensions cost families over $600,000 a day
articles.summary: A Michigan coal plant near Grand Rapids continues operations under a federal emergency order, incurring costs over $600,000 per day for families. This follows a court ruling against the government's actions, raising concerns from environmental groups about the financial and environmental impact.
articles.body: A 64-year-old coal-fired power plant near Grand Rapids, Michigan, will continue operating under a fresh federal emergency order, extending its life beyond the planned retirement date despite a court ruling against the administration's earlier actions.Energy Secretary Chris Wright issued the latest directive late Friday, requiring the J.H. Campbell Generating Plant to remain operational. The department said the facility was needed to protect electricity supplies and reduce the risk of blackouts.The extension is the seventh emergency order issued for the plant since May 2025. Environmental groups have challenged the repeated interventions, estimating that keeping the facility running costs Midwest households more than $600,000 every day, according to AP.Court ruling challenges federal interventionThe latest order follows a September decision by a three-judge panel of the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, which sided with environmental organisations and several states challenging the administration's directives.The court found that the government had not demonstrated an actual emergency under the law to justify keeping the plants operational. The ruling set aside the administration's previous actions as unlawful.The Energy Department has disputed the decision and petitioned for a rehearing before the full appeals court. A decision on whether the case will be reconsidered by the wider bench remains pending, with a possible appeal to the Supreme Court.Michigan, Illinois and Minnesota were among the states that joined environmental groups in challenging the orders.Despite the legal dispute, Wright has maintained that the Campbell facility and other coal-fired plants are necessary to protect electricity reliability. The administration has relied on emergency powers to prevent their scheduled closures.Environmental groups raise concerns over costsThe latest extension has drawn criticism from environmental organisations, which argue that the government has not demonstrated that the Michigan plant is needed to prevent a power shortage or has helped avert an outage.The Sierra Club estimates that keeping the facility operational adds more than $600,000 a day to costs borne by electricity customers across the Midwest.Its Burning Money tracker puts the total cost of federal orders extending the operating lives of fossil fuel plants in six states at more than $600 million. More than half of that amount is attributed to the Campbell plant in Michigan.Jessi Eidbo of the Sierra Club criticised the latest directive, saying: “At a time when prices are soaring and Americans are struggling to make ends meet, the Trump administration’s decision to issue yet another illegal and expensive extension is punishing.”Ted Kelly, director of US clean energy at the Environmental Defense Fund, also questioned the decision.“Instead of saving families’ money and letting the plant retire as planned, the Trump administration keeps putting its thumb on the scale for costly coal,” Kelly said.Trump administration continues push to support coal industryThe extension forms part of President Donald Trump's broader efforts to revive the US coal sector and maintain coal-fired electricity generation.In June, the administration announced plans to spend nearly $700 million supporting coal-fired power plants and coal exports. The Environmental Protection Agency has also repealed regulations limiting greenhouse gas emissions from coal- and gas-powered facilities.The agency, led by Administrator Lee Zeldin, is also seeking to restrict the ability of future administrations to regulate climate pollution from power plants.Wright has defended the use of emergency orders, arguing that keeping certain facilities operational is necessary to maintain a reliable electricity supply. Environmental groups and state governments, however, continue to challenge the legal basis and financial implications of those decisions.The dispute over the Campbell plant remains unresolved as the full appeals court considers whether to take up the case.You use AI every day. articles.title: JPMorgan Chase says software bug is fixed after thousands report issues with major U.S. banks
articles.summary: Users report bank outages from Chase, Bank of America and more of the nation's largest banking giants
articles.body:
Thousands of customers at major U.S. banks reported problems with their online accounts Monday after JPMorgan Chase said a software bug was affecting some transactions. The issue looked to have been fixed by late Monday.

The issue first emerged on Monday when Downdetector, a site that tracks user reports of outages for online services, showed that Chase, Bank of America, U.S. Bank, Wells Fargo, Capital One, Citi, TD Bank, USAA and American Express and others were spiking with user-reported issues.

In a statement posted to X , Chase said it was experiencing an issue linked to a software bug.

"JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems – there is no evidence this is cyber-related. It is taking longer than usual to service some customers," it said.

Chase said customers still had access to their accounts and funds.

Users of money transfer service Zelle also reported issues. A spokesperson for Early Warning Services, which owns Zelle, told the Associated Press that the network was fully operational.

"Other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us," a spokesperson for Chase added.

JPMorgan said Monday evening that it had resolved the issue, Yahoo Finance confirmed . Reports of issues on Downdetector had significantly tailed off.

It was the latest major consumer service outage in recent days, following Microsoft Outlook downtime last week. That outage lasted more than 30 hours , with the company blaming a network upgrade for the problem.

On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration had to institute a nationwide ground stop , causing thousands of flights to be delayed or canceled.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a team of experts from the FAA was inspecting a router that he said was the "likely cause" of the problem. He added that the ground stop was also connected to a server in Arkansas that "started to flood our network" while the FAA was in the process of upgrading its antiquated communications technology.

articles.title: Marina Muñoz, campeona del mundo de triatlón cross
articles.standfirst: La española, campeona de Europa, aventajó en 26 segundos a la francesa Paties, mientras que Eneko de Castro, plata, y Kevin Tarek, bronce, subieron al podio en categoría masculina
articles.summary: La española, campeona de Europa, aventajó en 26 segundos a la francesa Paties, mientras que Eneko de Castro, plata, y Kevin Tarek, bronce, subieron al podio en categoría masculina
articles.body: La española Marina Muñoz se ha proclamado campeona del mundo de triatlón cross al imponerse este martes en la prueba disputada en Abu Dabi con casi medio minuto de ventaja sobre la francesa Alizee Paties, que no pudo defender el título. Muñoz supo remontar para imponerse en la isla de Hudayriyat con un crono de 1.27:46 en el que cubrió 1 kilómetro de natación sin traje de neopreno en agua a 26,5 grados, dos vueltas a un circuito de bicicleta de montaña de 19,7 kilómetros y otras dos a un trazado de trail de 6,3 km, con 26 segundos de diferencia sobre la triatleta gala y 3:05 respecto a la bielorrusa Hanna Maksimava. La española, de 27 años, hizo valer su poderío en la carrera a pie, en la que corrió el tramo en 24:38 por el 25:20 de Paties, que no pudo resistir su ritmo. Muñoz, vigente campeona de Europa, había sido sexta en los Mundiales de 2021, donde logró el bronce sub-23, quinta en Ibiza 2023 y segunda tras Paties en Pontevedra 2025. En la prueba masculina Keller Norland logró el título élite y sub-23, al superar a los españoles Eneko de Castro, que llegaba con la vitola de vigente campeón mundial sub-23 en Pontevedra y oro europeo en julio en Banyoles, y Kevin Tarek Viñuela. El norteamericano, de 23 años y que se estrenaba en la prueba, relevó en el palmarés al francés Felix Forissier, campeón en Ibiza 2023 y Pontevedra 2025, tras revertir 22 segundos de desventaja respecto a De Castro. Norland paró el crono en 1h15:57 y precedió en 23 segundos a De Castro y en 39 a Viñuela, que revalidó el bronce de los pasados Mundiales. En categoría sub-23 femenina ganó la rusa Svetlana Chizhikova por delante de la mexicana María López y de su compatriota Vlada Khristoforova, y en la masculina el título y la plata fueron también para Norland y De Castro, y el bronce para el ruso Dmitrii Karpeev.

articles.title: Dozens injured after trains collide head-on in Prague
articles.summary: The low speed collision outside the Czech capital's main station triggered a massive emergency response.
articles.body:
Two trains have crashed outside Prague's main rail station, leaving dozens injured in the Czech capital.

The passenger trains collided head-on during rush hour at about 07:00 local time (06:00 GMT) on a bridge close to the station.

Forty-six people sustained injuries, with both train drivers among those said to be seriously injured, but fatalities were avoided as the trains were travelling at low speeds.

Transport minister Ivan Bednárik told local media: "I won't speculate on whether it was a technical fault or a human factor but so far it looks like a train ran a red light."

He continued: "Our goal is to thoroughly evaluate today's event and take any measures that will contribute to further increasing the safety of railway transport."

It took around two hours for emergency services to get all passengers off the trains.

Images from the scene showed rescue workers removing injured people on stretchers and emergency vehicles lined up around the station.

CTK, the Czech Republic's national news agency, said 16 foreign nationals were among those taken to hospital.

Police have since said the rescue operation was complete and an investigation was under way.

Other services to and from the station have been disrupted and passengers have been urged to use alternative routes.

articles.title: NHS data contract to stay with controversial US tech giant Palantir until 2029
articles.summary: Despite calls from some Labour MPs to end the arrangement with Palantir, ministers say a new contract will not be awarded until 2029.
articles.body:
The government says it will continue a key NHS data contract in England with the controversial US tech giant Palantir until 2029, rather than triggering an early release clause next year.

But ministers are inviting British firms to bid for the contract from 2029, with a procurement programme beginning next summer.

A Commons Committee had called on the government to part ways and appoint a company "more compatible with UK values". Protesters regularly target Palantir over Israel's use of its technology in the Gaza conflict and oppose its use in US immigration enforcement.

The £330m deal, which began in 2024 to help manage hospital waiting lists in England, was due to run until 2031.

The prime minister had faced pressure from some Labour MPs to cut ties with Palantir. They said they were extremely disappointed by the decision, calling the contract "an albatross" hanging around the NHS's neck.

The Liberal Democrats said the deal was "dangerous".

There have also been concerns raised about how patient data will be used .

Palantir, which was co-founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, has interests in US defence and security, and has contracts with the Israeli military.

Health minister James Frith said the move was "not about the politics of executives of suppliers, nor is it about the territories or customers that one company or one supplier makes".

The government says UK companies will be encouraged to tender to avoid overdependence on one supplier.

The timeframe is not fast enough for some members of the government.

Dame Chi Onwurah, Labour MP for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West, said the government needed to "act urgently" to procure "credible domestic alternatives".

"The government should not wait two years, it must start reducing this dependency now," she said.

Former Labour shadow chancellor John McDonnell went further, and accused Palantir of "human rights abuses". He said his constituents in Hayes and Harlington "expect the contract to be ended".

Liberal Democrat health spokeswoman Helen Morgan criticised the company for what she called its "appalling human rights record, run by an ally of Donald Trump".

The British Medical Association, which represents doctors, said it was glad the government had shown it was listening to its concerns about Palantir, but was frustrated the process of changing to another company was further delayed.

Palantir UK said it was right to press forward with the programme which was exceeding targets.

"We are proud of our work to date to help deliver more operations, speed up discharge and reduce the time patients need to wait to find out if they have cancer," Palantir UK senior vice-president Tom Watson said.

articles.title: UP polls: No consensus yet on Congress, SP seat-sharing talks, deferred after Rahul-Akhilesh meet
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress and Samajwadi Party are yet to reach a consensus on seat-sharing for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly elections, with a meeting
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress and Samajwadi Party are yet to reach a consensus on seat-sharing for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh assembly elections, with a meeting scheduled between the two parties on Tuesday deferred after discussions between their top leaders Rahul Gandhi and Akhilesh Yadav.The meeting is now expected to take place in the next two to three days as both sides work on a draft proposal and assess their respective seat-sharing formulas.Rahul and Akhilesh discussed the proposed alliance and seat-sharing during an interaction on Monday on the sidelines of the launch of Congress leader Sonia Gandhi's memoir, Belonging: A Journey Of Love, news agency PTI reported citing sources.A draft on seat-sharing was discussed during the conversation, but its details have not been made public. Leaders from both parties will now hold further deliberations based on the draft and the formulas proposed by their respective sides. Earlier, Akhilesh had confirmed that Congress wanted to contest on 181 seats.Congress sources said, as cited by PTI, that there was no agreement yet on the number of seats each party would contest. However, both sides have agreed that the allocation would be based on the "winnability" of candidates.A senior Congress leader said the discussions were not limited to deciding the total number of seats for each party. The two sides were also assessing which party had a better chance of winning individual constituencies to improve their overall electoral prospects.Congress says talks under way at leadership levelCongress leader and Uttar Pradesh in-charge Rajendra Pal Gautam said the discussions had already begun at the level of Rahul and Akhilesh.He said both leaders had given instructions to their respective party members and that groundwork was underway. Further discussions would follow before the allocation for individual constituencies was finalised.Akhilesh had said on Monday that formal seat-sharing discussions with the Congress had not yet begun. However, he maintained that the INDIA bloc would contest the Uttar Pradesh elections together.Congress steps up preparations for UP pollsThe Congress has planned to launch its election campaign in Uttar Pradesh in the first week of December. The campaign is expected to include rallies and various yatras.A meeting of senior Congress leaders was held at party president Mallikarjun Kharge's residence on Monday to discuss preparations for the assembly elections. The discussions focused on the party's electoral strategy, strengthening its grassroots organisation and its alliance with the SP.The Congress has also constituted a screening committee for the Uttar Pradesh elections, headed by senior leader Ajay Maken.The Uttar Pradesh assembly elections are expected to be held in February-March 2027.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Pope Leo says lung cancer surgery hasn’t changed his unity agenda
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV said his recent lung cancer surgery has not altered his agenda, outlook or even sense of mortality, as he projected a long pontificate focused on unity and healing within the church.
articles.body: Pope Leo XIV said his recent lung cancer surgery has not altered his agenda, outlook or even sense of mortality, as he projected a long pontificate focused on unity and healing within the church. Leo seemed full of health, energy and jokes during an airborne news conference on Monday while returning to Rome from Peru. The grueling, 12-day trip through three South American countries left several members of the travelling Vatican delegation and press corps sick. “I’m not 100% but I’m pretty good,” Leo said of his surgical recovery. “Endurance is one of the gifts the Lord gave me.” Leo, 71, had the lower lobe of his right lung removed Oct. 13 because of a cancerous tumor. He said it was discovered by chance during an annual checkup and appeared at first as a shadow on his lung. “The first news was a surprise. There were no symptoms. I felt fine,” he said. Once the cancer was confirmed, he decided to proceed immediately to have it removed, and said he hoped his experience would help others not fear having checkups or pursue preventive care. Prior to going into surgery, Leo said he saw no need to make provisions for the leadership of the Catholic Church if he were left medically impaired and unable to govern. He said he hadn’t written any instructions, as his predecessors had done, outlining the criteria under which he would resign, which some legal experts believe is necessary if a pope were to end up in an irreversible coma and unable to articulate his resignation. “Eventually I will do it, I think, but I don’t see the need now,” Leo said, adding that he never doubted he would be in good enough shape afterward to make the South America trip. He credited good doctors, prayer and what he described as a strong sense of determination to recover. Leo also showed himself in no hurry to appoint new cardinals who will eventually elect his successor, another sign that he is planning to be around for a while. “I will eventually get around to that,” he said. The pontiff also seemed in no hurry to get things done, saying he still doesn’t know what trips he’ll be taking next year — aside from his previously confirmed trip to South Korea to attend World Youth Day in August. Leo made it very clear that his No. 1 priority was “unity” and healing in the church, a reference to the polarization that has always existed but in some ways deepened during Pope Francis’ sometimes turbulent pontificate. Leo was asked, for example, whether he would consider ordaining married men to ease the priest shortage in the Amazon, where remote Indigenous communities can go months or longer without a priest to celebrate the sacraments. Amazonian bishops had asked Francis to allow for such a change but he declined. Leo said he had no plans to go down that path, either, saying the issue was too divisive. While ordaining married men is one solution to the priest shortage, Leo said “it’s a solution which in certain areas of the church can cause division because there is not universal, if you will, acceptance.” “One of my priorities is first to promote unity and communion among us as members in the church,” he said. “It may be in the future that some things will change. However for right now, for what I believe, an important part of my ministry of the church is to heal, bring people together,” he added. He similarly said he had no plans to change one of Francis’ most divisive decisions restricting the celebration of the old Latin Mass. Traditionalist Catholics had hoped Leo would be more sympathetic to their cause and would reverse Francis’ crackdown. But Leo said Francis’ decision already allowed for exceptions and that his decision stands. Where Leo did hint at some change was on the thorny issue of clergy abuse. He met with abuse survivors in Argentina and in Peru, and said he recognized that the issue of “spiritual abuse” was a problem in the church that needed to be addressed. For over two years, a Vatican working group has been studying “spiritual abuse,” given the increasing number of cases of people — often adult women — who accuse priests of using their spiritual authority to psychologically, physically or sexually abuse them. While the Catholic Church has laws punishing priests who sexually abuse minors, priests who use their spiritual authority to take advantage of people under their care rarely are sanctioned since there are no explicit laws criminalizing the practice. Leo, a canon lawyer, said he was aware of the loophole in the church’s canon law. “Spiritual abuse is a very serious topic in the church,” and needs to be addressed canonically, Leo said. “In order to exercise justice, you have to have a codification or a juridical expression of how to apply that, and that’s a very vague concept still,” he said. At the same time, he conceded that “we all probably could describe either specific cases or kinds of instances where that has happened.” One recent case of alleged spiritual abuse is expected to land soon on Leo’s desk. A Vatican-appointed tribunal is deciding the fate of the Rev. Marko Rupnik, a once-famous Jesuit mosaic artist accused by two dozen women of spiritual, psychological and sexual abuse. The women began complaining about his behavior in the 1990s, but nothing was ever done until the victims went public, amid suspicions he was protected by his Jesuit superiors, up to and including Francis.

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) on Tuesday revoked Stage III restrictions under the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) in
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) on Tuesday revoked Stage III restrictions under the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) in Delhi-NCR after the region’s daily average Air Quality Index (AQI) showed a downward trend, reaching 204.The CAQM’s sub-committee on GRAP decided to withdraw the restrictions imposed under Stage III.However, all measures under GRAP Stages I and II will continue to remain in force. Restrictions issued under the commission’s October 30 order will also continue, CAQM said.The October 30 order had directed preventive measures across Delhi-NCR from November 5 to 20, 2026, to control air pollution during the period of seasonal vulnerability.What restrictions will continue in Delhi-NCR?Under the October 30 order, dust-generating demolition and outdoor construction activities were restricted across the NCR, with exemptions for essential public infrastructure and specified projects, including railways, metro services, airports, hospitals, water supply and sanitation, and national security-related works.The order also directed state government and private offices in Delhi, Gurgaon, Faridabad, Sonipat, Ghaziabad and Gautam Buddha Nagar to operate with up to 50% of staff attending physically, while the remaining employees worked from home.Industrial establishments and essential services where such arrangements were not feasible were exempted.These restrictions will remain in force following the withdrawal of GRAP Stage III, as per the CAQM’s latest announcement.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: Markwayne Mullin flew from Washington to Louisiana to attend football game when thousands of flights were grounded: Report
articles.summary: US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin flew to Louisiana aboard a government aircraft to attend the LSU-Texas college football game on Saturday,
articles.body: US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin flew to Louisiana aboard a government aircraft to attend the LSU-Texas college football game on Saturday, at a time when thousands of passengers across the country remained stranded following a nationwide Federal Aviation Administration ground stop, the New York Post reported. Mullin is a native of Oklahoma and he atended Missouri Valley College, which makes it unclear as to why he had to attend the specific college football game.Mullin's trip came amid the continuing fallout from Friday's aviation disruption, which resulted in nearly 7,000 flight cancellations and around 8,000 delays. Some passengers faced travel disruptions lasting as long as 60 hours as airlines struggled to clear the backlog.The secretary attended the game at Tiger Stadium in Baton Rouge, where Texas staged a 12-point fourth-quarter comeback to defeat LSU. Other prominent attendees included actor Matthew McConaughey, influencer Alix Earle, former NFL quarterback Eli Manning and Republican Representative Steve Scalise.The trip drew attention because Mullin had been among the first officials to address reporters at the White House about the FAA crisis just a day earlier. He had said the nationwide shutdown was caused by a telecommunications outage and that there was no indication of a threat to the country.The secretary's use of a government aircraft was not considered an exception to the flight restrictions. According to a government source, the plane took off and landed nearly 24 hours after the FAA reopened US airspace, with no special exemptions granted for the flight. The Department of Homeland Security said Mullin is required by law to travel on government aircraft for security reasons, including access to secure communications and the need to ensure continuity of government in a national emergency.A DHS spokesperson said Mullin personally paid for the Louisiana trip, including his flights and game tickets, in accordance with the department's rules for personal travel.The New York Post report pointed out that Mullin was spotted in the private box of Ben Bordelon, the CEO of Bollinger Shipping, a Louisiana-based company that has billions of dollars in DHS contracts, including a recent $2.2 billion contract to build six icebreakers. articles.title: UK sanctions firms over Israeli West Bank settlements
articles.summary: It marks the first sanctions since the UK announced a tougher approach to Israeli actions in the territory.
articles.body:
The UK has sanctioned companies it said were involved in building settlements in the occupied West Bank, in the first package of measures since the government announced a tougher approach to Israeli actions in the territory.

The government said the sanctions against eight construction and property development firms would disrupt their flows of finance and ability to support building in the West Bank.

Settlements are illegal under international law, and there has been a rise in violence towards Palestinians in the West Bank by settlers in recent months.

It comes two days before the deadline for bids for construction tenders in the E1 area east of Jerusalem.

The plans, which have been condemned internationally, would in effect divide the West Bank in two and isolate East Jerusalem.

UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has said the E1 development would render a two-state solution "unviable" by "cutting through the heart of Palestine".

The sanctions also target Tzav 9, an Israeli activist movement which the UK government says has organised and carried out blockades to prevent aid entering Gaza.

It comes after the UK expanded its human rights sanctions regime last month, enabling the government to sanction individuals and companies involved in violations of international humanitarian law anywhere in the world.

The government is also developing separate legislation to ban the import of settlement goods and the provision of advertising services for settlement properties in the UK.

Miliband said: "Protecting the two-state solution is the North Star of this government's approach.

"That is why my message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution.

"The status quo in the West Bank and Gaza is unacceptable.

"We are committed to working productively with a new Israeli government and the Palestinian Authority to advance lasting peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians alike."

UK announces sanctions on West Bank settlements prompting furious Israeli response

Israel opens up bids for highly sensitive West Bank settlement project

In September, the UK government announced that it would ban the import of goods from Israeli settlements, as well as acting against companies and individuals providing services for settlement expansion.

At the time, Miliband said the move marked the "beginning of a new approach" to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, which "not only calls out injustice and suffering but acts".

Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.

There has been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.

articles.title: Khurda admin orders action against highway-parked trucks
articles.summary: Khurda admin orders police, RTO and NHAI to crack down on illegal truck parking on national highways, urging use of terminals at Godipada and Kuhudi.
articles.body: Bhubaneswar: The Khurda administration has directed police and transport authorities to step up enforcement and take strict action against truck drivers for parking their vehicles illegally on highways.In a letter issued on Tuesday, the administration asked the police, regional transport officer and the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) to intensify patrolling and enforcement measures to prevent unauthorised roadside parking of goods vehicles, particularly along national highways.The administration noted that despite the operationalisation of truck terminals at Godipada and Kuhudi from Oct 27, many goods vehicles continue to be parked along roadsides, creating traffic hazards and increasing the risk of accidents. “Indiscriminate parking of trucks on highways poses a serious threat to road safety, obstructs smooth movement of traffic and increases the risk of fatal accidents,” the letter stated.According to police sources, 286 and 287 fatalities were reported on highways in Khurda district between 2024 and 2025.The terminals were set up to provide designated parking space for heavy vehicles and discourage their stoppage on highways. Truck operators have been advised to use these designated facilities instead of parking vehicles along roadsides.Authorities have been asked to create awareness among truck owners and drivers about the availability of the designated truck terminals while simultaneously cracking down on violations. “Cases of unauthorised roadside parking should be dealt with strictly under the provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988,” the administration said.Recently, the state govt directed authorities to plug systemic safety gaps on national highways following a spate of fatal accidents. Citing the Supreme Court’s interim directions issued on April 13, 2026, the transport department has reminded agencies that “no heavy or commercial vehicle shall park or stop on any national highway carriageway or paved shoulders except at designated bays, laybys or wayside amenities.”The transport department has asked the Odisha police to immediately form dedicated highway surveillance teams for patrolling and enforcing the ban on illegal parking and stoppages.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Bhubaneswar | Silver Rate in Bhubaneswar | Bank Holidays in Bhubaneswar | Public Holidays in Bhubaneswar | Petrol Price in Bhubaneswar | Diesel Price in Bhubaneswar | CNG Price in Bhubaneswar | LPG Price in BhubaneswarStay updated with the latest Bhubaneswar news.
